subject: ⛅️ Neocloud's silver lining
body_text:
96 
Plus: $2T budget gap | Tuesday, October 20, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
 Presented By Barclays Investment Bank 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Oct 20, 2026
 
 
 🎩 A good Tuesday to you. A bounce in the AI trade yesterday put some spring in the market's step, but there's still a pebble in that shoe.

 This morning, U.S. stock futures are down after a rough day of trading in most Asian markets. Shares of South Korean neocloud Elice fell 30% in their market debut, sparking new AI trade skittishness . 🗓️ Today, Matt looks at the flip side of that worry — some analysts think the CoreWeave bond sell-off may be less than meets the eye.

 And Emily brings the skinny on the growing costs of paying the interest on Uncle Sam's rapidly expanding debt. Go! 1,005 words, a 4-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: A neocloud's silver lining
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: Tradeweb; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Goldman Sachs has raised its rating on the shares of CoreWeave to a "buy" recommendation after a brutal week for the data center operator.

 Why it matters: That view may come as a surprise given that the tumble in CoreWeave bonds and stock last week had appeared to encapsulate all of what markets fear about the debt-dependent AI boom : too much money, most of it borrowed, chasing returns that may prove elusive. 

 Zoom out: What's cloudy (sorry!) about the outlook for CoreWeave and the other data center operators known as neoclouds, as well as their much bigger rivals, the hyperscalers, is that nobody really knows how profitable all these data centers will eventually be. 

 But if the cost of borrowing to build them goes up — which is what the spike in CoreWeave's bond yields suggests — that should make them less profitable . The latest: Goldman analyst Gabriela Borges argued in a note yesterday that the increase in borrowing costs that CoreWeave ultimately faces will be less substantial than the company's yippy bond yields might suggest. 

 What they're saying: " Our discussions suggest that CoreWeave's unsecured spreads (currently at 13.5-15.0%) are not representative of what CoreWeave's true cost of new debt is; in fact, the unsecured bond market has already been closed to new CoreWeave issuance for several months," she wrote, meaning that the company can't issue new unsecured bonds anyway, so those yields won't be representative of what it will pay when it needs to borrow more.

 What will it pay? Well, CoreWeave's primary way of tapping the capital markets for cash it needs to build data centers now, Borges says, is by borrowing in the fast-growing project finance market. Zoom in: Project finance debt is a niche that developed as a way to fund giant infrastructure projects that required a lot of upfront investment, like power plants. 

 Such projects require a lot of upfront investment during the risky construction phase, but pay off only over the long term. How it works: A standalone corporate entity, known as a special purpose vehicle — legally separate from the "sponsor" companies that actually want the project built — is created that has legal control over the project.

 The SPV is provided with a little bit of equity from the sponsors. This legal entity is then, typically, able to leverage that equity at a higher rate than it would be if it was technically part of its sponsor companies. For heavily indebted sponsor companies, such as CoreWeave, project finance debt can also carry a lower interest rate. The big picture: AI-related issues have transformed the project finance market in recent years, a separate Goldman Sachs report on credit markets noted on Oct. 15. 

 AI issues dominate the $106 billion in project finance debt issued so far this year. That's nearly triple the $37 billion issued last year. Yes, but: The boom in the project finance market also suggests that a hefty chunk of risk related to the AI boom continues migrating to complex corners of the market where it might be tougher to track. 

 The bottom line: The emergence of the AI project finance market could mean CoreWeave has a bit more financial flexibility than its bonds — currently at yields of about 15%, still in distressed territory — would indicate.

2. The deficit is getting real expensive
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred , U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures. 

 Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession. 

 The deficit is being driven partially by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war. By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data.

 That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion). Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

 Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates —  a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021.

 Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget. The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office.

 At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking Bush's infamous "Read my lips: no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing reelection. Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts. What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called bond vigilantes might still press for it.
